name: Reliance Controls 31406CRK Pro/Tran Manual Transfer Switch Kit
summary: The default answer for a 5,000 to 7,500 watt portable generator with an L14-30 outlet and a short list of must-run circuits.
verdict: The 31406CRK is the transfer switch most electricians reach for when a homeowner shows up with a portable generator and asks for a safe way to connect it. Reliance builds it as a small prewired panel that mounts beside your main breaker panel, with a flexible conduit whip that enters the panel through a knockout. Six chosen circuits are moved onto it, and each gets a three-position switch: Line, Off and Gen. Because every circuit is switched individually, power from the generator can only go to those circuits and never back out onto the utility lines. The CRK suffix means the kit version, which adds Reliance's PB30 outdoor power inlet box and a 30-amp generator cord, so you plug the generator into the outside wall rather than running cords through a window. It is rated for 30-amp, 120/240-volt generators with an L14-30 outlet. Six circuits is enough for a furnace, refrigerator, freezer, sump pump and a couple of lighting or outlet circuits in a typical home.
skipIf: Six circuits fills up fast once 240-volt loads take two positions
pros: Six selectable circuits covers the essentials in most houses
Each circuit has its own Line/Off/Gen switch, so you cannot energize the utility lines by design
Kit format bundles the PB30 inlet box and a 30-amp cord
Pre-wired whip shortens the electrician's install time
Pairs with the most common portable generator outlet, the L14-30
cons: Six circuits fills up fast once 240-volt loads take two positions
Still needs a licensed electrician and usually a permit

name: Reliance Controls 31410CRK Pro/Tran Manual Transfer Switch Kit
summary: Buy it if your must-run list includes a 240-volt well pump or you simply have more than six essential circuits.
verdict: The 31410CRK is the ten-circuit sibling of the 31406CRK, built the same way: a prewired switch panel that sits next to your main panel, a whip into the panel, and a separate Line/Off/Gen switch for every circuit you move across. The reason to pay more is not power. Both kits are 30-amp, 120/240-volt units, and your generator's running watts still decide how much you can run at once. The reason is positions. A 240-volt load such as a well pump uses two of them, and once you add a furnace, refrigerator, freezer, sump pump, kitchen outlets and some lighting, six positions are gone before you get to the home office or the garage door opener. Ten positions also give you more freedom to balance 120-volt loads across the two legs of the generator, which keeps one side from overloading while the other loafs. Like the six-circuit kit, the CRK version adds the PB30 inlet box and a 30-amp cord.
skipIf: More circuits does not mean more power; the generator is still the limit
pros: Ten circuit positions leaves room for 240-volt loads like a well pump

Lets you split loads across both legs of the generator more evenly
Worth the step up when the six-circuit list is already full
cons: More circuits does not mean more power; the generator is still the limit
Larger enclosure needs more wall space next to the panel
Easy to over-wire circuits you will never run at once

name: Reliance Controls TF151W Furnace Transfer Switch
summary: The cheapest legitimate way to keep the heat on in an outage if the furnace is the only thing you truly need.
verdict: In cold climates the most important load in an outage is usually the gas or oil furnace, which needs only a few hundred watts for its blower, inducer and controls but needs it hardwired. The TF151W exists for exactly that. It is a single-circuit, 15-amp, 120-volt transfer switch that replaces or sits beside the furnace's service switch, so the furnace can run either from its normal circuit or from a generator connected to the switch. There is no need to move circuits at the main panel and no need for a 240-volt generator, which makes it a good match for a small inverter generator. That is also its limit: it powers the furnace and nothing else. If you also want the refrigerator, freezer and sump pump, a six-circuit switch like the 31406CRK covers the furnace and those loads together, and costs less than buying several single-circuit switches. Have an electrician confirm it suits your furnace and local code.
pros: Purpose-built for one job: running a gas or oil furnace on a generator
Mounts at the furnace instead of at the main panel
Simple switch between utility and generator power
Far less money and labor than a whole panel switch
Works with smaller generators and inverter generators
cons: Your refrigerator, sump pump and lights still need another plan
Some furnaces are fussy about generator power quality and grounding

name: Reliance Controls PB30 Power Inlet Box
summary: The inlet to buy for a 30-amp setup, especially if you are installing an interlock rather than a Reliance kit.
verdict: A power inlet box is the part of a generator hookup that lives outside: a weatherproof box on the wall with a male inlet where the generator cord plugs in. The PB30 is Reliance's 30-amp version, with an L14-30 inlet that mates with the matching connector on a standard 30-amp, four-wire generator cord. Inside the house it is wired to either a manual transfer switch or, with an interlock kit, a dedicated generator breaker in the main panel. If you buy a Reliance CRK kit you already have one, so do not buy it twice. Where it earns its own place in this list is the interlock route: interlock kits supply the panel hardware, not the inlet, so you need an inlet box regardless. Mount it where the generator can sit outdoors well away from windows, doors and vents, and keep the cord run reasonably short. The male inlet cannot be energized unless the cord is connected to a running generator, which is exactly why the inlet is male and the cord end is female.
skipIf: Only half of the system; it does nothing without a switch or interlock
pros: Lets the generator plug in at an outside wall, not through a window
Standard L14-30 inlet matches most mid-size portables
Weatherproof enclosure with a hinged cover
Works with manual transfer switches and listed interlock kits alike
Same box the Reliance CRK kits include
cons: Only half of the system; it does nothing without a switch or interlock
Buy it separately only if your switch kit does not already include one
Needs wiring back to the switch by an electrician

name: Reliance Controls PBN50 Power Inlet Box
summary: Only for generators with a 50-amp, 125/250-volt outlet; for everything else the PB30 is the right box.
verdict: Large portable generators, usually around 9,000 running watts and up, often carry a 50-amp, 125/250-volt California-style twist-lock outlet alongside or instead of the L14-30. The PBN50 is Reliance's inlet box for that connection. On paper a 50-amp, 240-volt circuit can carry up to 12,000 watts, which is enough to run central air on a large portable or several big loads at once, but only if the whole path is rated for it: generator outlet, cord, inlet, wiring and the switch or interlock breaker. A 50-amp inlet feeding a 30-amp switch gains you nothing. That makes the PBN50 most useful with a panel interlock, where the generator breaker can be sized to the generator, or with a 50-amp-rated transfer switch. Check the generator's outlet before buying, because a 50-amp cord will not mate with an L14-30 outlet, and adapters that change amperage are a bad idea on a circuit like this.
skipIf: Pointless with a generator that only has an L14-30
pros: 50-amp capacity for large portables with a CS6369 outlet
Lets an interlock or 50-amp switch use the generator's full output
Weatherproof outdoor enclosure
Same male-inlet safety logic as the 30-amp box
Future-proofs the wall if you may buy a bigger generator
cons: Pointless with a generator that only has an L14-30
Needs heavier wire, which means more install cost
50-amp cords are thick, heavy and expensive

name: Reliance Controls PC3020 30-Amp Generator Power Cord
summary: Worth buying when the kit cord is too short to keep the generator a safe distance from doors and windows.
verdict: Most transfer switch kits include a 10-foot cord, which is often too short to put the generator where it should be: outdoors, well clear of windows, doors, vents and the garage. The PC3020 is Reliance's 20-foot, 30-amp generator cord, with an L14-30 plug at the generator end and a matching L14-30 connector at the inlet end. It is a four-conductor cord, which a 120/240-volt hookup needs, and the twist-lock ends hold firmly. A cord like this is also the honest answer to the most dangerous question in generator ownership, which is whether you can just make a cord with two male ends and plug it into a dryer outlet. You cannot. A cord with a female end at the house and a male inlet on the wall is the safe version of that idea. If you need more distance than 20 feet, ask your electrician whether a longer 30-amp cord or a relocated inlet makes more sense, because voltage drop rises with length and thin cords overheat.
skipIf: Twenty feet may still be shorter than the safe placement you want
pros: Twenty feet lets the generator sit farther from the house
L14-30 ends match the PB30 inlet and most mid-size portables
Four-wire cord carries both hots, neutral and ground
Twist-lock ends do not pull out under their own weight
Made by the same company as the inlet box
cons: Twenty feet may still be shorter than the safe placement you want
A heavy cord to coil and store
Redundant if your kit's cord already reaches
